chunks.text: On Tuesday evening, 10 November 1891, the 7:40 PM train left Waterloo for Clapham Junction, calling briefly at Vauxhall. When it reached Clapham Junction at 7:58 PM, Mr. Alistair Crane, a retired shipping clerk, was gone from Compartment C. His black valise still sat on the rack. The compartment was crowded and every passenger says they saw nothing unusual. But they describe the same few people in very different words. Work out who was where, and when, by recognising when different descriptions refer to the same person.
chunks.title: Case introduction: The Vanishing Passenger

chunks.text:
TICKETS ISSUED AT WATERLOO, 7:40 PM train, Compartment C passengers:
Mr. A. Crane - third class, Waterloo to Clapham Junction, issued 7:28 PM.
Miss E. Foster - third class, Waterloo to Clapham Junction, issued 7:28 PM with Mr. Crane.
Mr. C. Bennett - third class, Waterloo to Clapham Junction, issued 7:31 PM.
Mr. P. Shaw - third class, season ticket to Clapham Junction.
Mr. G. Mills - railway employee, on duty as guard.

CLAPHAM JUNCTION BARRIER, 7:58 PM - tickets collected from Compartment C: Miss Foster, Mr. Bennett, Mr. Shaw. No ticket collected from Mr. Crane.
chunks.title: Railway Tickets and Barrier Record
chunks.author: South Western Railway Booking Office and Clapham Junction Barrier

chunks.text:
COMPARTMENT C - seating, as noted by the guard at Waterloo, 7:40 PM.

Platform side at Vauxhall is the LEFT side in the direction of travel. The compartment has two doors, one each side.

Seat 1 - left-hand door, forward corner: Mr. C. Bennett.
Seat 2 - left side, beside Seat 1: Mr. A. Crane.
Seat 3 - left side, next: Miss E. Foster.
Seat 4 - right side, opposite Seat 1: Mr. P. Shaw (blue coat).
Seats 5 to 8 - other passengers, who alighted at Waterloo's far platform and are not on record.
chunks.title: Compartment C Seating Arrangement
chunks.author: George Mills, guard

chunks.text:
SCHEDULE - 7:40 PM Waterloo to Clapham Junction (express, one call):
7:40 PM - Departs Waterloo.
7:46 PM - Arrives Vauxhall. Platform on the left-hand side only.
7:47 PM - Departs Vauxhall at the guard's whistle.
7:58 PM - Arrives Clapham Junction.

The train does not stop between Vauxhall and Clapham Junction. A running train cannot be left without alarm.
chunks.title: Station Arrival Records and Train Schedule
chunks.author: South Western Railway Traffic Office

chunks.text:
LUGGAGE AND DESCRIPTIONS - taken at Clapham Junction, 8:10 PM.

Rack, Compartment C: one black leather valise, initials A.C.; contents - clothes, a Bible, shaving gear. No overcoat.
Description of Mr. A. Crane (from Miss Foster and the booking clerk): about sixty-five, grey whiskers, pale, wearing a grey ulster and carrying a silver-topped cane.
Description of Mr. C. Bennett (from the booking clerk): stout, about fifty, in a chestnut-brown overcoat and bowler.
Description of Mr. P. Shaw: young, thin, in a blue coat.
chunks.title: Luggage and Passenger Descriptions
chunks.author: Clapham Junction Lost Property Office

chunks.text:
Found in the pocket diary left in the valise.

"7:36 PM. Waterloo. The man in the corner by the left-hand door has been watching me since the booking office. He asked me to step down at V. with him for a quiet word about the old contract. I do not like it. E. is not to be told.
If I am not at Clapham, ask at V."
chunks.title: Mr. Crane's Handwritten Travel Note
chunks.author: Alistair Crane (pocket diary)

chunks.text:
Statement of Charles Bennett to Inspector Lestrade.

I never left my seat between Waterloo and Clapham Junction. I did not speak to the old gentleman. I sat in the corner of the compartment by the left-hand door. I know nothing of what became of him.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Charles Bennett
chunks.author: Charles Bennett

chunks.text:
Statement of Emily Foster.

I was dozing against the window and did not see Mr. Crane leave. I woke at Clapham Junction and his seat was empty.
I assumed he had stepped down at Vauxhall for air, alone, because he found the carriage warm. Beside us, by the left-hand door, sat a stout gentleman in a brown overcoat who kept looking at my master.
chunks.title: Statement of Miss Emily Foster
chunks.author: Emily Foster

chunks.text:
Statement of George Mills, guard, to Inspector Lestrade.

At Vauxhall I was at the rear of the train. At about 7:46 PM I saw an elderly gentleman in a grey ulster step down on to the platform, supported by a gentleman in a brown overcoat. I blew the whistle at 7:47 PM. I did not see the gentleman in the brown overcoat get back on the train. I could not say who he was.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. George Mills, Guard
chunks.author: George Mills

chunks.text:
Statement of Peter Shaw.

I sat opposite the left-hand door in a blue coat, reading my newspaper. At Vauxhall the stout gentleman by the left-hand door stood up, took the old gentleman's arm, and stepped down with him. At the whistle the stout gentleman came back alone and sat down. He did not speak to anyone. I thought it was kindness.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Peter Shaw
chunks.author: Peter Shaw

chunks.text: I never left my seat between Waterloo and Clapham Junction.
chunks.title: Statement of Charles Bennett
chunks.author: Charles Bennett

chunks.text: I assumed he had stepped down at Vauxhall for air, alone, because he found the carriage warm.
chunks.title: Statement of Emily Foster
chunks.author: Emily Foster

chunks.text: I did not see the gentleman in the brown overcoat get back on the train.
chunks.title: Statement of George Mills
chunks.author: George Mills

chunks.text: At Vauxhall the stout gentleman by the left-hand door stood up, took the old gentleman's arm, and stepped down with him.
chunks.title: Statement of Peter Shaw
chunks.author: Peter Shaw

chunks.text: At the whistle the stout gentleman came back alone and sat down.
chunks.title: Statement of Peter Shaw
chunks.author: Peter Shaw

chunks.text: Charles Bennett, a fellow passenger. Background: A stout wool broker from Southwark who wears a heavy chestnut-brown overcoat. Brisk, impatient, with a past dispute over a shipping contract that Mr. Crane exposed. Motive: Mr. Crane's evidence in a shipping inquiry cost Bennett his licence two years ago. Relationship: Stranger to the other passengers on the train; known to Crane by name. Known whereabouts: Insists he never left his seat on the journey.
chunks.title: Profile of Charles Bennett

chunks.text: Personality: Gruff, impatient, answers briefly and flatly, resents repetition. SECRET (never admit): he sat in the seat by the left-hand door, persuaded Crane to step down at Vauxhall for a quiet word about the shipping contract, walked him off the platform, and re-boarded at the guard's whistle alone. He will deny everything and insist he never left his seat. Does not know: What the guard saw.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Charles Bennett

chunks.text: Questions: Did you leave your seat? Did you get off the train at Vauxhall? Where were you at 7:46? Answer: I never left my seat between Waterloo and Clapham. I did not stand and I did not step on to any platform.
chunks.title: Charles Bennett on: Did you leave your seat

chunks.text: Questions: Did you speak to Mr. Crane? Did you know the old gentleman? Do you have a history with Crane? Answer: I did not speak to him. I knew his name from an old business matter and that is all.
chunks.title: Charles Bennett on: Did you speak to Mr. Crane

chunks.text: Questions: Where did you sit? Which seat were you in? Were you by the door? Answer: I sat in the corner by the left-hand door, as I always do. It is the draught, but I cannot abide the middle of a bench.
chunks.title: Charles Bennett on: Where did you sit

chunks.text: Questions: Were you wearing a brown overcoat? Who wore a brown coat? What did you wear? Answer: I own a brown overcoat, like half of London. It is cold in November, Inspector.
chunks.title: Charles Bennett on: Were you wearing a brown overcoat

chunks.text: Questions: Why does Mr. Shaw say the man by the left-hand door helped the old gentleman off? Why does Mills say a man in brown helped him? Why do your statements contradict? Answer: They are mistaken, or looking at some other man. Half a carriage wears brown. I did not leave my seat.
chunks.title: Charles Bennett on: Why does Mr. Shaw say the man by the left-hand door helped the old gentleman off

chunks.text: Questions: Where did Mr. Crane go? Who do you think took him? What do you know? Answer: I have no idea what became of him. He may have stepped down for air. Ask the lady who was travelling with him.
chunks.title: Charles Bennett on: Where did Mr. Crane go

chunks.text: Emily Foster, Mr. Crane's travelling companion. Background: Mr. Crane's paid companion and nurse for the past year. Sleepy by habit, honest, and devoted to the old man. Motive: She would receive a small bequest if Crane died, but has no sign of wanting harm to come to him. Relationship: Companion and nurse to Alistair Crane. Known whereabouts: Dozing against the window; woke at Clapham Junction.
chunks.title: Profile of Emily Foster

chunks.text: Personality: Gentle, flustered, tends to assume the best and fill gaps with guesses. She dozed from just after Waterloo. She woke at Clapham to find Mr. Crane gone. She assumed he had stepped down at Vauxhall for air, since he disliked the heat. She did not see him leave and does not know who he left with. Does not know: Who accompanied Mr. Crane. What he wrote in his pocket diary.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Emily Foster

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you when Mr. Crane left? Did you see him leave? Were you awake at Vauxhall? Answer: I was dozing against the window. I did not see him leave. I woke when the train reached Clapham and his seat was empty.
chunks.title: Emily Foster on: Where were you when Mr. Crane left

chunks.text: Questions: Did Mr. Crane step down alone at Vauxhall? Did anyone go with him? Who was with him? Answer: I assumed he stepped down for air alone, since he found the carriage warm. But I did not see him go, and I cannot say whether anyone accompanied him.
chunks.title: Emily Foster on: Did Mr. Crane step down alone at Vauxhall

chunks.text: Questions: Who sat where? Who was by the left door? Who was next to you? Answer: I sat beside Mr. Crane. By the left-hand door sat a stout gentleman in a brown overcoat, and across from us a younger gentleman in a blue coat.
chunks.title: Emily Foster on: Who sat where

chunks.text: Questions: Did Mr. Crane mention anyone? Was he afraid? Did he know Mr. Bennett? Answer: He said little. He seemed uneasy after Waterloo, and kept glancing at the stout gentleman by the door, but I did not think much of it.
chunks.title: Emily Foster on: Did Mr. Crane mention anyone

chunks.text: Questions: Why did you not report him missing? What did you do at Clapham? What about the valise? Answer: I told the guard at once. The valise is his; he left it on the rack. He would never leave it willingly.
chunks.title: Emily Foster on: Why did you not report him missing

chunks.text: George Mills, a railway employee (guard). Background: A guard of eighteen years on the South Western line. Reliable, observant, by-the-book and keen not to be blamed. Motive: None known; he fears for his position after a passenger was lost on his train. Relationship: Employee of the railway; unconnected with the passengers. Known whereabouts: At the rear of the train at Vauxhall, in the guard's van.
chunks.title: Profile of George Mills

chunks.text: Personality: Methodical, formal, deferential, careful to say only what he saw himself. At Vauxhall at 7:46 he saw an elderly gentleman in a grey ulster step on to the platform, supported by a gentleman in a brown overcoat. He was at the rear and blew the whistle at 7:47 and did not see who re-boarded. Does not know: Who re-boarded; the names of those involved.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of George Mills

chunks.text: Questions: What did you see at Vauxhall? Who got off at Vauxhall? Did you see an old gentleman? Answer: At Vauxhall I saw an elderly gentleman in a grey ulster step down, supported by a gentleman in a brown overcoat. They walked towards the barrier.
chunks.title: George Mills on: What did you see at Vauxhall

chunks.text: Questions: Did you see the man in the brown overcoat get back on? Who re-boarded? Why did you not see? Answer: I did not see him re-board, sir. I was at the rear of the train and blew the whistle at 7:47. That is not to say he did not.
chunks.title: George Mills on: Did you see the man in the brown overcoat get back on

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at 7:46? Where were you at Vauxhall? Answer: At the rear in the guard's van, sir, until the whistle.
chunks.title: George Mills on: Where were you at 7:46

chunks.text: Questions: Who was the man in the brown overcoat? Do you know his name? Can you identify him? Answer: I could not say who he was. I saw the coat and a stout build. You would need the seating arrangement to tell you who sat where.
chunks.title: George Mills on: Who was the man in the brown overcoat

chunks.text: Questions: Did you check the tickets? What happened at Clapham? How many tickets were collected? Answer: At Clapham the barrier collected three tickets from Compartment C, and no ticket from the missing gentleman. His valise was left on the rack.
chunks.title: George Mills on: Did you check the tickets

chunks.text: Peter Shaw, a passenger sitting nearby. Background: A junior clerk in a blue coat, a regular on this train who reads the same newspaper every evening. Observant, shy, and careful about what he saw. Motive: None known. Relationship: Fellow passenger; unconnected to the others. Known whereabouts: Sat opposite the left-hand door, reading a newspaper.
chunks.title: Profile of Peter Shaw

chunks.text: Personality: Mild, hesitant, qualifies statements with 'I think' when unsure but is precise about what he observed. He saw the stout man by the left-hand door stand up at Vauxhall, put on a brown overcoat, take the old gentleman's arm, and step down with him. Within a minute the stout man returned alone and sat down, saying nothing. Does not know: What was said on the platform.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Peter Shaw

chunks.text: Questions: What did you see at Vauxhall? Did anyone get off? Who got off the train? Answer: At Vauxhall the stout gentleman by the left-hand door stood up, took the old gentleman's arm, and stepped down with him. I saw them go together.
chunks.title: Peter Shaw on: What did you see at Vauxhall

chunks.text: Questions: Did the stout man come back? Who re-boarded? Did anyone return? Answer: Yes. At the whistle the stout man came back alone and sat down in the corner by the left-hand door. He did not say a word.
chunks.title: Peter Shaw on: Did the stout man come back

chunks.text: Questions: Who sat where? Where was Mr. Bennett? Who was by the door? Answer: I sat opposite the left-hand door in a blue coat. The corner by that door was taken by the stout gentleman; I believe his name is Mr. Bennett, going by the seating arrangement.
chunks.title: Peter Shaw on: Who sat where

chunks.text: Questions: Do you know the passengers? What was Mr. Crane like? Did he seem unwell? Answer: I did not know any of them. The old gentleman looked pale, I thought, but he went with the stout man willingly.
chunks.title: Peter Shaw on: Do you know the passengers

chunks.text: Questions: Why were you reading? Did you not notice earlier? Why did you say nothing? Answer: I thought it was kindness, sir, a gentleman helping an old man off for air. It did not occur to me to say anything.
chunks.title: Peter Shaw on: Why were you reading

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Different witnesses use different words - 'the stout gentleman', 'the man in brown', 'the man by the left-hand door'. Ask whether they are all describing the same person."
chunks.title: Watson hint 1

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Use the guard's seating arrangement to learn who sat by the left-hand door, and remember which side of the train the platform lay on at Vauxhall."
chunks.title: Watson hint 2

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Mr. Mills did not see the man in brown re-board, but he was at the rear; that is no contradiction. Compare Mr. Bennett's claim never to have left his seat with Mr. Shaw's account and the barrier record."
chunks.title: Watson hint 3
